lead: Watershed segmentation imagines an image as a landscape. Grey level is height. Bright pixels are high ground and dark pixels are valleys. Rain falls and each valley fills with water. When two pools meet, a dam is built along the meeting line. That line is the watershed. The method separates touching coins, cells and machine parts. The input is usually a gradient image, not the raw photo, so flat object centres stay low and object edges form high ridges. Markers stop noise from creating thousands of tiny pools.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for the gradient image, and Unit 2 and Unit 3 for the morphological opening and closing used to build markers.

blocks.text: Take a grey image f(x,y). x and y are pixel coordinates; f is the grey level. Treat f as height on a map. A bright pixel is a hill. A dark pixel is a valley. A regional minimum is a connected set of pixels with the same low value whose neighbours are all higher. Rain collects in each regional minimum. The set of pixels that drain to one minimum is a catchment basin. Where two basins touch, a dam is drawn. The dam is the watershed line. The line sits on ridges, not in valleys.

blocks.where: g is the gradient magnitude; Gx and Gy are the horizontal and vertical derivatives at pixel (x,y).

blocks.text: A raw photo is a poor landscape. A flat object interior may be dark and a flat background bright, so flooding starts inside the object and grows past the true boundary. The correct input is a gradient image. On this surface, flat object centres are valleys and object edges are ridges. Flooding then stops near edges. See Chapter 4.2. Noise is the main danger. Every tiny dip in g becomes a regional minimum, and each one starts a basin. A noisy gradient can give hundreds of regions. This failure is over-segmentation.

Markers are pixels known to lie inside an object or in the background. They tell the flood where to start. Internal markers mark object centres. External markers mark background. With markers, the algorithm does not flood from every regional minimum; it floods only from the marked minima. The watershed line then separates the marked objects.

Two common ways to find internal markers are the h-minima transform and a morphological opening. The h-minima transform removes regional minima whose depth is less than h. Depth is the height difference between the minimum and the lowest saddle that leads out of it. A larger h removes more shallow minima and gives fewer regions. Morphological opening is f ∘ b, with f the gradient image and b a small structuring element, often a disk or a 3×3 square. Opening deletes bright features smaller than b. On a gradient it erases thin bright ridges, so two nearby basins join and the shallower minimum disappears into the deeper one. Dark dips themselves are filled by a closing, not by an opening; the h-minima transform is the direct way to suppress them.

External markers can be found by taking the watershed of the gradient and keeping only the watershed lines as background seeds. Another route is the distance transform for a binary object. For each object pixel p, D(p)=min distance from p to a background pixel. D is small near the object border and large near the object centre. Touching objects have multiple maxima in D. Flood the negative distance transform, -D. The maxima of D become minima of -D. Flooding -D with watershed lines between the maxima is one way to split touching objects. Watershed itself is also called the watershed transformation, and some syllabi describe it through the Meyer flooding algorithm: scan grey levels from low to high, dilate labelled basins inside a mask, and build a dam where two labels meet.

items: Smooth the image lightly to reduce noise. Do not remove real edges.
Compute the gradient magnitude with Chapter 4.2.
Find internal markers. Use h-minima on the gradient, or an opening, or a distance transform for binary objects.
Find external markers. One way is the watershed of the gradient; its lines are background seeds.
Modify the gradient so the only minima are at the markers. A common rule is to set marker pixels to the minimum grey level.
Run watershed flooding on the modified gradient.
Remove very small regions and merge regions that are too similar. This is region merging, covered in Chapter 4.5.

blocks.text: The output is a label image. Each basin has a different label. Watershed lines can have a separate label. Use the labels for counting cells, separating coins, or finding defects. A Chennai factory checking washers can use distance-transform watershed to separate washers that touch on a conveyor. A hospital can use marker-controlled watershed to split overlapping cells in a blood smear.

examples.question: A 1-D grey profile has values 9, 7, 3, 7, 9, 8, 3, 7, 9 at x = 1 to 9. Show the flooding levels, the two basins and the watershed line.
steps: Find regional minima. x=3 has value 3 and is lower than its neighbours. x=7 has value 3 and is lower than its neighbours. The minima are at x=3 and x=7, both at level 3.
At level L=3, basin A starts at x=3 and basin B starts at x=7.
At L=7, the left basin includes x=2,3,4 because f(2)=7 and f(4)=7. The right basin includes x=7,8 because f(8)=7. x=6 has f(6)=8, so it is still dry.
At L=8, the right basin adds x=6 because f(6)=8. The left basin adds nothing.
At L=9, the left basin reaches x=1 and x=5. The right basin reaches x=5 and x=9. Both basins reach x=5 at the same level, so x=5 becomes the watershed line.
Final basin A is {1,2,3,4}, size 4. Final basin B is {6,7,8,9}, size 4. The watershed line is at x=5.
examples.answer: Basin A has 4 pixels, basin B has 4 pixels, and the watershed line is at x = 5; the two regional minima are at x = 3 and x = 7.
examples.check:
xs = list(range(1, 10))
f = [9, 7, 3, 7, 9, 8, 3, 7, 9]
mins = [xs[i] for i in range(1, len(f)-1) if f[i] < f[i-1] and f[i] < f[i+1]]
left, right = mins[0], mins[1]
A = []
B = []
W = []
for x, val in zip(xs, f):
    dl = abs(x - left)
    dr = abs(x - right)
    if dl < dr:
        A.append(x)
    elif dr < dl:
        B.append(x)
    else:
        W.append(x)
print(len(A))
print(len(B))
print(W[0])
print(left)
print(right)

traps: Running watershed on the raw image instead of the gradient. Flat dark interiors and brightness noise start many basins, so the output is badly over-segmented. Use the gradient magnitude as the flooding surface.
Forgetting that every shallow noise dip is a regional minimum. Smoothing alone does not remove all of them. Use h-minima, an opening, or markers to suppress shallow minima.

Using markers as seeds but leaving other minima in the gradient. Extra basins still appear. Marker-controlled watershed must make the markers the only minima, for example by setting marker pixels to the minimum grey level.
Sign error with the distance transform. To split touching objects, flood the negative distance transform -D. The maxima of D are object centres; they must become minima for flooding.
Confusing the watershed line with the object boundary. The line separates basins. With good markers it approximates the boundary, but small regions still need merging and cleaning.

quiz.q: What image is used as the flooding surface in watershed segmentation, and why?
quiz.a: The gradient magnitude. Flat object interiors give low values and object edges give high ridges, so basins stop near boundaries.

quiz.q: Why does watershed on a raw noisy image over-segment?
quiz.a: Every small dark dip is a regional minimum. Flooding starts in each one, so many tiny basins form.

quiz.q: A 1-D profile has values 8, 4, 6, 3, 7 at x = 1 to 5. Find the watershed line and the two final basins.
quiz.a: Regional minima are x=2 with value 4 and x=4 with value 3. At level 6 both basins reach x=3, so x=3 is the watershed line. Final basins are {1,2} and {4,5}, sizes 2 and 2.

quiz.q: A colleague gets 300 regions from a noisy gradient. State two fixes and why each works.
quiz.a: Use the h-minima transform to delete minima whose depth is below h; that removes noise seeds. Apply a closing to the gradient to fill small dark dips, or an opening to delete thin bright ridges so shallow basins merge into deeper neighbours. Either way fewer basins start, and marker control limits flooding to known seeds.

quiz.q: Define catchment basin and watershed line.
quiz.a: A catchment basin is the set of pixels draining to one regional minimum. The watershed line is the ridge where two basins meet.

quiz.q: Why is the negative distance transform used to split touching coins?
quiz.a: Distance transform D is large at coin centres and small at borders, so its maxima are centres. Flooding -D turns those maxima into minima, so watershed lines fall between touching coins.

quiz.q: Gradient values along a line are 2, 5, 9, 5, 2. If markers are at x=1 and x=5, where is the watershed line?
quiz.a: The markers are the only minima. Flood from x=1 rightwards and from x=5 leftwards. They meet at x=3, the highest point. The watershed line is x=3.

quiz.q: Compare watershed on the raw image, on the gradient alone, and on a marker-controlled gradient.
quiz.a: Raw image floods from dark flat interiors and noise, giving wrong and many regions. Gradient alone stops at edges but still floods from every noise minimum. Marker-controlled gradient uses known seeds, so only marked objects are separated and over-segmentation is controlled.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice watershed is used in microscopy cell counting, industrial inspection and medical organ segmentation. Modern pipelines often use watershed as a post-processing step after a deep network produces a probability map. Search terms: marker-controlled watershed, h-minima transform, Meyer flooding, distance transform segmentation, cell nuclei watershed.
